extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of constitutional law and political science; statesmen and legislators
extracted.subtask_description: Analytical exposition of political jurisdiction and the structure, powers, and principles of the United States federal constitution, aimed at explaining institutional design and its effects. Covers impeachment/political jurisdiction, division of powers, legislative bicameralism, and the executive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose of political jurisdiction
rubrics_metrics.description: The main object of the political jurisdiction which obtains in the United States is ... to deprive the citizen of an authority which he has used amiss, and to prevent him from ever acquiring it again.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presented as an administrative measure sanctioned by judicial formalities; characterizes American political jurisdiction as aimed at removal/prevention of authority rather than traditional criminal punishment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mixed system for removing public functionaries
rubrics_metrics.description: They have surrounded the act which removes a public functionary with the securities of a political trial; and they have deprived all political condemnations of their severest penalties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains the American compromise: removal is procedurally securitized (trial-like) but stripped of the harsh criminal penalties common in Europe; this produces different social effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Senate jurisdiction over civil officers; military exception
rubrics_metrics.description: American constitutions subject all the civil functionaries to the jurisdiction of the senate, while the military ... are exempt from that tribunal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notes institutional allocation: civil officials answer to Senate impeachment/tribunal; military officers are dependent on the chief magistrate and thus treated differently in removal/discipline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Political jurisdiction as preventive rather than punitive
rubrics_metrics.description: The principal object of the political tribunals of Europe is to punish the offender; the purpose of those in America is to deprive him of his authority. A political condemnation in the United States may ... be looked upon as a preventive measure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argues US political condemnations remove capacity/power rather than inflict corporal or criminal punishment; therefore judges are not restricted to exact criminal definitions and political offences are broadly described.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vagueness/breadth of political offence definitions increases severity
rubrics_metrics.description: Nothing can be more alarming than the excessive latitude with which political offences are described in the laws of America. Article II., section iv.: '...impeachment for, and conviction of, treason, bribery, or other high crimes and misdemeanors.' Many state constitutions are even less explicit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides examples (Massachusetts: 'misconduct or mal-administration'; Virginia: 'mal-administration, corruption, or other high crimes') and warns that broad or unspecified offences create virtually unlimited political responsibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniformity between accusers and judges favors party vindictiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: In the United States the tribunal which passes sentence is composed of the same elements, and subject to the same influences, as the body which impeaches the offender, and that this uniformity gives an almost irresistible impulse to the vindictive passions of parties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains a structural risk: if the same political actors prosecute and judge, convictions may be more certain even if penalties are milder, amplifying partisan retribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Risk of majority tyranny through political jurisdiction
rubrics_metrics.description: By preventing political tribunals from inflicting judicial punishments, the Americans seem to have eluded the worst consequences of legislative tyranny, rather than tyranny itself; and I am not sure that political jurisdiction, as it is constituted in the United States, is not the most formidable which has ever been placed in the rude grasp of a popular majority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Warns that easily invoked removal powers, even if less physically severe, can enable a majority to dominate officeholders continuously; suggests monitoring impeachment frequency as a sign of degeneration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Division of authority: states as rule, federal government as exception
rubrics_metrics.description: The obligations and the claims of the federal government were simple and easily definable ... the government of the states remained the rule, and that of the confederation became the exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains constitutional design: federal powers are enumerated and limited; powers not enumerated belong to states; practical disputes over limits motivated creation of federal judiciary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Federal judiciary to maintain balance of power
rubrics_metrics.description: A high federal court was created, which was destined, among other functions, to maintain the balance of power which had been established by the constitution between the two rival governments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notes the judiciary's role is to resolve federal-state boundary questions; the text also remarks the court's action is often indirect (jurisdictional/interpretive rather than direct governance).

rubrics_metrics.name: Enumerated federal prerogatives (external relations and general interests)
rubrics_metrics.description: The exclusive right of making peace and war, of concluding treaties of commerce, of raising armies, and equipping fleets, was therefore granted to the Union. The Union was invested with the power of controlling the monetary system, of directing the post-office, and of opening the great roads ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Further examples: power to legislate on bankruptcy, grant patents; federal authority over external affairs and some general internal interests; federal taxation powers to fulfill engagements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constraints on states (ex post facto and nobility)
rubrics_metrics.description: The states were forbidden to enact ex post facto laws, or to create a class of nobles in their community.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are specific constitutional prohibitions intended to protect union-wide principles and prevent state abuses that could compromise the Union's security.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle: when federal exclusive right not exercised, states may legislate
rubrics_metrics.description: Whenever the exclusive right of regulating certain matters is not reserved to congress by the constitution, the states may take up the affair, until it is brought before the national assembly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gives example (bankruptcy law): if Congress neglects to make a general law, each state is free to legislate for itself; notes this point has been settled through court discussion (jurisprudence).

rubrics_metrics.name: Bicameral legislature as compromise between state independence and national sovereignty
rubrics_metrics.description: The federal legislature of the Union was composed of a senate and a house of Representatives. The principle of the independence of the states prevailed in the formation of the senate, and that of the sovereignty of the nation predominated in the composition of the house of representatives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains representational effects: each state sends two senators (state-equality principle) while representatives are apportioned by population (national-majority principle); this middle course reconciles conflicting interests but can produce tensions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Different modes, terms, and functions of the two houses
rubrics_metrics.description: The house of representatives is named by the people, the senate by the legislators of each state; the term for representatives is two years, that of senators is six. The functions of the house are purely legislative (impeachment by the House); the senate tries impeachments, ratifies treaties, and approves appointments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Highlights structural safeguards and checks: double versus single election, staggered terms, distinct powers (House initiates/presents impeachments; Senate is tribunal and advice-and-consent body).

rubrics_metrics.name: Executive design: elective, responsible, stable, and accountable presidency
rubrics_metrics.description: The president is an elective magistrate ... chosen for four years, and he may be re-elected ... he was made the sole representative of the executive power of the Union; the senate takes cognizance of his relations with foreign powers, and of the distribution of public appointments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describes the balance sought: an executive dependent on the people's will but possessing sufficient stability and strength; Senate oversight limits corruption but cannot compel executive action; salary fixed at entry; suspensive veto exists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Centralization of union in certain respects
rubrics_metrics.description: In the Union there is but one tribunal to interpret, as there is one legislature to make the laws; and an impost Voted by the representatives of the nation is binding upon all the citizens.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compares to European monarchies/provinces to show that, despite being a confederation of republics, the Union exercises strong central authority in law interpretation and national taxation.
